pages.title: Logistics Chassis
pages.text: By now the network is a bit of a mess. A $(item)Logistics Chassis$() is a pipe that does several jobs at once, so we can collapse what we have.$(br2)Open the $(item)Compiler$() and start unlocking $(thing)Chassis$().

pages.title: Modules, Not Pipes
pages.text: A Chassis does nothing by itself — you add $(thing)modules$() to give it jobs. There are five tiers, and the only difference between them is how many modules they hold.$(br2)Build the program for a $(item)Chassis Mk2$(), which fits two, and craft a few.$(br2)Replace one of the Basic pipes on a storage chest with a Chassis, then open it with the $(item)Pipe Manager$().

pages.title: ItemSink Modules
pages.text: The two slots at the top are for modules. Craft an $(item)ItemSink Module$(), add it, and click the $(thing)[!]$() beside it to configure it exactly like the pipe it replaced.$(br2)Then replace the Basic pipe holding the default route with another Mk2 Chassis, add an ItemSink Module, and set that module as the default route.

pages.title: Polymorphic ItemSink
pages.text: The $(item)Polymorphic ItemSink Module$() cannot be given a list of items. Instead it automatically sinks whatever is $(italic)already$() in the chest behind it.$(br2)Used liberally these make chest storage fast and effortless. Replace the rest of your storage Basic pipes with Mk2 Chassis and Polymorphic sinks.

pages.title: Provider Modules
pages.text: Now consolidate the provider side: craft $(item)Provider Modules$() and add them to the same Chassis.$(br2)Their settings let you include or exclude specific items, but the one that matters here is $(thing)Excess Inventory$() at the bottom.

pages.title: Excess Inventory
pages.text: $(li)$(thing)Normal$() — provide everything$(li)Leave first stack$(li)Leave last stack$(li)Leave first & last stack$(li)Leave 1 item per stack$(li)Leave 1 item per type

pages.title: Which Setting
pages.text: A Chassis with a Polymorphic sink must keep at least one of each item, or it stops sinking that item and it starts going elsewhere — so $(thing)Leave 1 item per type$() is ideal there.$(br2)$(thing)Normal$() suits machine output buffers and regular ItemSink modules. $(thing)Leave 1 item per stack$() helps when you want specific slots reserved for specific items.$(br2)Tip: configure a whole stack of fresh modules at once by holding them and right-clicking in the air. Careful — once configured, modules no longer stack.

pages.title: Cleaning Up
pages.text: With Provider Modules in place, remove the old $(item)Provider Pipes$(). This matters more than it looks: while both exist they provide the same items twice, and the network double-counts them.$(br2)Provider Pipes have the same settings as Provider Modules, incidentally — we skipped them earlier because Normal was fine.

pages.title: Which Way Is It Facing?
pages.text: A Chassis attaches to exactly $(italic)one$() thing at a time, shown by orange dots on one side. Yours may well have latched onto the Power Junction or a hopper instead of the chest.$(br2)Fix it by holding $(thing)shift$() and right-clicking the Chassis with the Pipe Manager.

pages.title: Crafting Modules
pages.text: The furnace sits idle most of the time, so let's have it smelt gold as well as iron. Craft two $(item)Crafting Modules$() and an Mk2 Chassis to replace the Crafting Pipe underneath it.$(br2)Set them up one per recipe, just like the pipe. Both still need the Satellite Pipe — but since Satellites have no recipes of their own, both modules can share one.

pages.title: Item Bouncing
pages.text: Two crafts sharing one machine can collide. Request iron and gold in quick succession: the iron ore arrives and starts smelting, then the gold ore arrives to find the top occupied and the Satellite fails to insert it.$(br2)The gold ore $(thing)bounces$() — back into the network and off to storage. The Crafting Pipe knows, and asks again once the top is free.

pages.title: Why Providers Matter
pages.text: Bouncing is the reason it is crucial to have providers everywhere that can sink items.$(br2)If an ingredient bounces and lands somewhere that does $(italic)not$() provide it back to the network, the Crafting Module can never finish — it cannot re-request an ingredient that is no longer reachable.

pages.title: Sneaky Upgrades
pages.text: $(thing)Upgrades$() alter what a pipe already does, rather than adding new jobs like modules, and they work in many pipe types rather than only Chassis. Managing them needs a $(item)Pipe Controller$() — it looks like a red Pipe Manager.$(br2)A $(item)Sneaky Upgrade$() makes a pipe pretend it is on a $(italic)different$() side of the thing it is attached to when inserting.

pages.title: Retiring the Satellite
pages.text: That is exactly the furnace problem. With a Sneaky Upgrade on the Chassis holding the Crafting Modules, it can insert into the top of the furnace by itself.$(br2)Right-click the Chassis with the Pipe Controller, install the upgrade, and click the $(thing)[!]$() beneath it. A 3D view of the furnace opens: drag with the left mouse button to rotate, then right-click the top face.

pages.title: Testing It
pages.text: The 3D view closes without confirming anything, which is poor feedback — but you can check by crafting.$(br2)Remove the Satellite Pipe, update the Crafting Modules' recipes to stop using it, and request an iron ingot.$(br2)This works because the Sneaky Upgrade changes the side the Chassis $(italic)inserts$() into, not the side it $(italic)extracts$() from — so the Chassis must stay on the bottom.
